title: "What would the UK gain from closer ties with the EU? Trade, productivity and investment gains from deeper UK–EU integration"

  In September 2026 the Prime Minister said that all options for the UK's relationship with the EU are on the table, from the current Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) to full membership. We provide comparable estimates of what each option would be worth to the UK relative to the TCA, combining a meta-analysis of 37 gravity studies, a general equilibrium model of world trade, and evidence on productivity and on business investment lost since the referendum. Through lower trade costs in goods and services, re-joining the EU would raise UK real income by 1.6%, and by 1.8% with productivity effects. If membership also brought back the lost investment, the long-run gain would be 3.7%, or 2.9% if that shortfall would have narrowed anyway; about three-quarters of it would arrive within 15 years of accession. An EEA/Swiss-type agreement, a deep free trade agreement or a customs union would be worth 1.3–1.8%. How much lost investment an agreement brings back depends on its legal permanence: how hard it would be to undo. In goods trade a customs union and an EEA/Swiss-type agreement deliver similar gains, but a customs union would oblige the UK to apply the EU's external tariff, including any tariff on imports from China, and once services and investment are counted the EEA/Swiss-type agreement is ahead.
  </details>

Ten years after the referendum, every option for the UK's relationship with
the EU is back on the table. In September 2026 the Prime Minister said the
options run from the current Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) to full
membership, and in October told the House of Commons that after the UK–EU
summit in Brussels on 20 November the two sides should start a dialogue about
the long-term relationship. This paper puts
the options on one scale, measured from the TCA. It pools 37 gravity studies
(3,554 estimates) to measure the trade effect of each type of agreement, solves
a general equilibrium model of world trade covering 81 economies, and adds
services trade, the productivity effects of trade liberalisation and the
recovery of business investment held back since the referendum.

![Where the gains come from: long-run UK real-income gain relative to the TCA, by layer. Bars show goods trade, services trade, productivity and investment recovery net of its cost; brackets show the range when 22–93% of the investment shortfall is due to uncertainty; triangles show the total with the 2025 US tariffs and an EU tariff on all imports from China.](../files/du-shepotylo-2026-uk-eu-gains-by-layer.png){fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart of the long-run gain in UK real income relative to the TCA, split into goods trade, services trade, productivity and investment recovery. EU membership 3.67%, EEA/Swiss-type agreement 1.79%, deep free trade agreement 1.54%, customs union 1.26%, sectoral landing (veterinary agreement and mutual recognition) 0.85%."}

| Agreement | Lower trade costs, goods and services | Long run, with productivity and investment |
|---|---|---|
| EU membership | +1.59% | +3.67% (£112bn a year) |
| EEA/Swiss-type agreement | +0.66% | +1.79% (£54bn) |
| Deep free trade agreement ("TCA Plus") | +0.74% | +1.54% (£47bn) |
| Customs union | +0.46% | +1.26% (£38bn) |
| Sectoral landing (veterinary agreement and mutual recognition) | +0.30% | +0.85% (£26bn) |

: UK real-income gain relative to the TCA; £bn a year at 2025 GDP. A breakdown of the TCA (no deal, WTO terms) would cost 0.70% of real income, about £21 billion a year, from goods trade alone.

## Key findings

- **Membership gives the largest gain under every assumption tested**: 1.6%
  of real income from lower trade costs in goods and services, and **3.7%,
  about £112 billion a year**, in the long run once productivity and the
  recovery of lost investment are counted. Lower trade costs alone would raise
  UK goods exports to the EU by about 40%.
- **The trade-cost gains are the best-measured part.** Productivity and
  investment roughly double them but rest on judgements: if the 13.6%
  shortfall in business investment would have narrowed anyway under the TCA,
  membership would be worth 2.9%.
- **Legal permanence matters as well as depth.** Agreements that are harder to
  undo bring back more of the investment held back by uncertainty. That is why
  an EEA/Swiss-type agreement ranks first among the partial options in 85% of
  the 5,751 combinations of assumptions tested.
- **Services access matters as much**: an EEA-type agreement with full access
  is worth 2.34%, a Swiss-type agreement without it 1.25%.
- **A customs union ties the UK to EU trade policy.** In goods trade it is level
  with an EEA/Swiss-type agreement (0.42% each), but if the EU taxed all of its
  imports from China at the US rate it would fall 0.29 percentage points
  behind, and unwinding the UK's own trade agreements outside the EU could
  lower it further.
- **The gains take time; the 2025 US tariffs change little.** If the UK
  re-joined in 2035, output would be 1.5% higher at accession and 2.8% higher
  by 2040, with about three-quarters of the long-run gain arriving by 2050.

## What this means for each option

The paper does not recommend an option — that choice also turns on
sovereignty, budget contributions, free movement and what the EU would agree,
which the estimates do not price. It shows what each option is worth and which
features would make it worth more.

- **Membership** gives the largest gains under every assumption, and brings a
  vote on EU rules, budget contributions and free movement.
- **An EEA/Swiss-type agreement** keeps UK trade policy independent. Its value
  rises with services access, and an EEA-type agreement is the stronger form.
- **A customs union** is a conditional option: its value depends on EU trade
  policy towards third countries, over which the UK would have no vote.
- **A deeper TCA** is strong on trade, but unless it is anchored in more
  permanent institutions it brings back less of the lost investment. The
  near-term reset agenda — the veterinary agreement, emissions-trading linkage
  and [mutual recognition of conformity assessment](/research/papers/mrca-streamlining-standards.qmd)
  — is worth banking while the longer-term choice is made.
- **Across all options**, the government should compare the choices on the
  same basis, against the TCA, and report the better-measured gains from lower
  trade costs separately from the larger but less certain gains from
  productivity and investment.
